name: Montirelin

angle.text: Montirelin is a stable TRH analogue that appears in peptide and nootropic discussions as a wakefulness and neuroprotection compound, with some users linking alertness to staying consistent with training and routines. The appearance link is speculative; it has been studied in animals for arousal, with essentially no human trial data.

summary: A lab-stable TRH analogue studied in animals for arousal and neuroprotection; essentially no human trial data.
note: Animal and cell data only; no approval stated.
currentQuick:
Montirelin is a modified version of TRH built to last longer and act more strongly in the brain.
It has been tested in rodents and cell cultures for memory, arousal and neuroprotection. Human evidence is limited to a brief reported study in patients with impaired consciousness.
How it works: It binds TRH receptors, raising TSH and prolactin and stimulating cholinergic, noradrenergic and dopaminergic activity in animal brains.[3][5][8]
Risks and caveats: No safety profile in healthy people has been published in the sources reviewed. Animal studies report effects on blood pressure and heart rate, and its endocrine actions mirror TRH.[7] It is not described as an approved drug.
deepLead:
Montirelin (CG-3703, NS-3) is a synthetic analogue of thyrotropin-releasing hormone (TRH) designed to be more stable, longer acting and more centrally active than the natural hormone. Wikipedia traces its origins to patents held by the German company Gruenenthal.
Published work describes effects on arousal, memory, neuroprotection and neurotransmitter turnover in laboratory animals and cultured cells. The Wikipedia article reports a human study in patients with neurological disturbances but states no regulatory approval; no source reviewed documents appearance-related use.

name: Glypromate

angle.text: Glypromate (GPE) is an IGF-1-derived tripeptide discussed in peptide circles for brain protection and recovery, which some users tie to better focus and consistency. It has no documented appearance use; the evidence is laboratory neuroprotection research, and its analogue trofinetide became an approved Rett syndrome drug.

summary: The IGF-1-derived tripeptide GPE, a neuroprotection research compound whose analogue trofinetide became an approved Rett syndrome drug.
note: Experimental; no human trials of the unmodified peptide located.
currentQuick:
Glypromate is a three-amino-acid piece of IGF-1. In lab research it has been examined as a neuroprotective and anti-inflammatory agent.
It is chiefly of interest as the parent of trofinetide. Nothing in the sources reviewed links it to a documented appearance benefit.
How it works: It is thought to act in brain tissue as a neuroprotective signal derived from IGF-1; because the plain peptide is rapidly degraded, more stable analogues were developed.[1]
Risks and caveats: Experimental and not approved. No human safety data for the unmodified peptide were found in the sources reviewed.
deepLead:
Glypromate, also called GPE (glycine-proline-glutamate), is a tripeptide that corresponds to the N-terminal fragment of insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1). It is described as having anti-inflammatory and neuroprotective properties in laboratory research.
The natural tripeptide crosses the blood-brain barrier poorly and is broken down quickly, so researchers have developed more stable analogues; the best known is trofinetide, approved in 2023 for Rett syndrome. No clinical trial of glypromate itself is described in the sources reviewed, and no source documents appearance-related use.

name: Trofinetide

angle.text: Trofinetide is an approved prescription drug for Rett syndrome and a GPE analogue, so it comes up in peptide discussions as a relative of Glypromate. No appearance use is documented; it is used as a disease treatment and studied in that setting.

summary: The first approved Rett syndrome drug, a GPE analogue; a disease treatment with no appearance use documented.
note: Approved only for Rett syndrome; common GI side effects.
currentQuick:
Trofinetide is an oral prescription drug for Rett syndrome. It is a stabilised copy of a small IGF-1 fragment and was approved by the US FDA in 2023.
It entered peptide catalogues because of its relation to GPE, but its evidence concerns a rare neurological disease, not appearance.
How it works: It is thought to dampen neuroinflammation and support neuronal signalling through IGF-1-related pathways, without fixing the gene mutation behind Rett syndrome.[12]
Risks and caveats: Diarrhea and vomiting are the most common adverse effects in trials.[11][12] It is prescription-only, with limited data in kidney impairment.
deepLead:
Trofinetide (brand names Daybue, Daybue Stix; Daybu in the EU) is an oral prescription medicine for Rett syndrome, a rare genetic neurodevelopmental disorder, in patients aged two years and older. The US FDA approved it in March 2023, the first drug approved for the condition.
It is a synthetic analogue of glycine-proline-glutamate (GPE), the N-terminal tripeptide of IGF-1, and was developed by Neuren Pharmaceuticals and then commercialised by Acadia Pharmaceuticals. It was first explored for neuroprotection, for example in stroke. Its approval rests on a 12-week placebo-controlled phase 3 trial. It is a treatment for a specific disease; no source reviewed documents an appearance-related use.

name: Fosgonimeton

angle.text: Fosgonimeton is an investigational Alzheimer's drug that acts as a prodrug of dihexa, a compound popular in nootropic circles. It was developed for dementia rather than any cosmetic purpose, and no appearance data exist; the evidence is limited to clinical research on cognition.

summary: Investigational Alzheimer's drug (a dihexa prodrug) with no appearance data.
note: Investigational only; not approved anywhere.
currentQuick:
Fosgonimeton is an investigational drug from Athira Pharma that was tested for Alzheimer's disease. It is described as a prodrug of dihexa that boosts HGF/MET signaling.
It has no studied role in appearance. It is a related name in research-compound discussions.
How it works: It is described as a positive modulator of the HGF/MET neurotrophic pathway, reported in preclinical studies to promote neuronal health and cognition-related effects.
Risks and caveats: It is not approved for any use. A phase I trial reported on safety and tolerability in volunteers and Alzheimer's patients; details of later-phase results are in the primary literature.
deepLead:
Fosgonimeton (also ATH-1017 or NDX-1017) is an investigational small molecule developed by Athira Pharma as a prodrug of an active metabolite, dihexa, that enhances signaling of hepatocyte growth factor (HGF) at its MET receptor.  It was studied as a possible treatment for Alzheimer's disease and other dementias rather than for any cosmetic purpose.
In looksmaxxing and longevity-oriented communities it appears mainly as a related name to the research peptide-like compound dihexa. It is not an approved medicine anywhere.
Published human data consist of a phase I trial in healthy volunteers and people with Alzheimer's disease and a registered phase 2/3 trial; the rest of the literature is preclinical.

name: BNN-20

angle.text: BNN-20 is a DHEA-derived "microneurotrophin" discussed in research-chemical circles for brain protection. It has no documented appearance use; the evidence is preclinical, mainly Parkinson's mouse models, with no human data.

summary: Preclinical DHEA-derived BDNF mimic studied in Parkinson's mouse models; no human data.
note: Animal data only; not approved for any use.
currentQuick:
BNN-20 is a lab-made steroid-like compound intended to mimic the brain growth factor BDNF. It has been tested only in animal and cell models of Parkinson's disease.
No human studies exist and it has no studied appearance role.
How it works: Reported to act through the TrkB receptor, the BDNF receptor, and to reduce neuroinflammation in mouse models.
Risks and caveats: Human safety is unknown because no clinical trials are published. It is not an approved drug.
deepLead:
BNN-20 is a synthetic compound described by its developers as a "microneurotrophin": a small molecule, 17-beta-spiro-[5-androsten-17,2'-oxiran]-3beta-ol, derived from the hormone DHEA, that crosses the blood-brain barrier and is reported to lack endocrine side effects. 
Research has been preclinical, mainly in the "weaver" mouse model of Parkinson's-like dopamine neuron loss.  It is discussed in longevity and nootropic circles as a neurotrophin mimic; it has no approved use.

name: BNN-27

angle.text: BNN-27 is a DHEA-derived NGF mimetic described by its developers as lacking hormonal activity, and it is discussed in research-chemical circles for nerve and brain protection. No appearance use is documented; the evidence is preclinical with no human data.

summary: Preclinical NGF-mimicking DHEA analogue; no human data.
note: Animal data only.
currentQuick:
BNN-27 is a lab-made steroid-like molecule meant to imitate nerve growth factor. It has been studied only in cells and animals.
No human trials or appearance research exist.
How it works: Reported to activate TrkA and p75NTR, the NGF receptors, without DHEA's hormonal effects.
Risks and caveats: Human safety is unknown; it is not an approved drug.
deepLead:
BNN-27 (17alpha,20R-epoxypregn-5-ene-3beta,21-diol) is a synthetic neurosteroid analogue of DHEA described as a "microneurotrophin" and an NGF mimetic.  It is reported to be a selective, high-affinity agonist of the TrkA and p75NTR receptors, to cross the blood-brain barrier, and to lack hormonal activity. 
Evidence is preclinical; in mouse models it showed neuroprotective and neurogenic effects.  It has no approved use and no studied appearance role.

name: N-Acetyl Selank Amidate

angle.text: This acetylated, amidated Selank analogue is sold as a research chemical, with users hoping for calmer mood and more social ease than the parent peptide. The appearance link is indirect and anecdotal; the analogue itself has no direct studies, and the evidence relates to Selank.

summary: Acetylated, amidated Selank analog sold as a research chemical; no direct studies.
note: No direct studies; not approved.
currentQuick:
N-Acetyl Selank Amidate is a chemically modified version of the peptide Selank. The modifications are meant to make it last longer in the body.
No studies of this exact compound are reported, and it has no studied appearance use.
How it works: It is presumed to act like Selank, which is described as modulating GABAergic signaling; this has not been tested for the modified form.
Risks and caveats: It is sold for laboratory use and is not approved for human use in most jurisdictions. Safety in people has not been studied.
deepLead:
N-Acetyl Selank Amidate is a synthetic heptapeptide analog of Selank, with the sequence Ac-Thr-Lys-Pro-Arg-Pro-Gly-Pro-NH2, N-terminally acetylated and C-terminally amidated. These changes are described as intended to resist enzymatic breakdown. 
It is sold by research-chemical suppliers for laboratory use and is not approved for human therapeutic use. Claimed benefits are extrapolated from Selank research; the source reports no direct studies of this variant.

name: N-Acetyl Semax Amidate

angle.text: This acetylated, amidated Semax analogue is sold as a research chemical, with users seeking sharper focus and stamina than the parent peptide. Any appearance link runs through habit consistency and is anecdotal; the analogue itself has no direct studies, and the evidence relates to Semax.

summary: Acetylated, amidated Semax analog sold as a research chemical; no direct studies.
note: No direct studies; not approved.
currentQuick:
N-Acetyl Semax Amidate is a chemically modified version of the peptide Semax. The modifications are meant to make it last longer in the body.
No studies of this exact compound are reported, and it has no studied appearance use.
How it works: It is presumed to act like Semax, which is described as affecting neurotrophin (BDNF, NGF) expression in animal studies; this has not been tested for the modified form. Intranasal use is the route typically described.
Risks and caveats: It is sold for laboratory use and is not approved for human use in most jurisdictions. Safety in people has not been studied.
deepLead:
N-Acetyl Semax Amidate is a synthetic heptapeptide analog of Semax, with the sequence Ac-Met-Glu-His-Phe-Pro-Gly-Pro-NH2, N-terminally acetylated and C-terminally amidated. These changes are described as intended to resist enzymatic breakdown. 
It is sold by research-chemical suppliers for laboratory use and is not approved for human therapeutic use. Claimed benefits are extrapolated from Semax research; the source reports no direct studies of this variant.

name: DNSP-11

angle.text: DNSP-11 is an experimental GDNF-derived peptide discussed in nootropic circles for dopamine neuron support. No appearance use is documented; it has been studied only in rats and monkeys, with no human trials.

summary: An experimental GDNF-derived brain peptide studied only in rats and monkeys, with no human trials and no appearance data.
note: Preclinical only; no human studies found.
currentQuick:
DNSP-11 is an 11-amino-acid peptide derived from a precursor region of GDNF, a protein that supports dopamine neurons. It was developed as a smaller candidate for Parkinson's disease research.
Published studies are in cells, rats and rhesus macaques. No human trials were found, and nothing in the sources links it to appearance outcomes.
How it works: Researchers propose that processing of the GDNF precursor yields small peptides such as DNSP-11, which in rat experiments changed dopamine neuron function and increased ERK 1/2 signalling in cells.
Risks and caveats: Its safety in humans has not been studied in published trials. It is not an approved drug, and animal studies do not establish human effects.
deepLead:
DNSP-11 (dopamine neuron stimulating peptide-11) is an experimental 11-amino-acid peptide that researchers derived from the pro-region of glial cell line-derived neurotrophic factor (GDNF). It was proposed as a smaller, easier-to-deliver alternative to full-length GDNF, which has shown protective effects on dopamine neurons in animal models and in some Parkinson's disease trials but is difficult to deliver to the brain because of its size .
Published work on DNSP-11 consists of cell-culture and animal studies, including rats and rhesus macaques, in which the peptide has been given directly to the brain or repeatedly through the nose . No human clinical trial of DNSP-11 appears in the sources reviewed here. It is not an approved drug, and the sources contain no evidence about any effect on appearance.
The compound is discussed in this wiki because it is a neurotrophic peptide of the kind that appears in longevity and nootropic peptide catalogues. The sources reviewed contain no looksmaxxing forum discussion of it.

name: FGL

angle.text: FGL is a synthetic fragment of a neural adhesion protein discussed in nootropic circles for memory and brain plasticity. No appearance use is documented; the evidence is rodent memory data with no human trials.

summary: A lab-made fragment of a neural adhesion protein with rodent memory data and no human trials or appearance evidence.
note: Preclinical only; no human studies found.
currentQuick:
FGL is a 15-amino-acid peptide taken from NCAM, a protein involved in nerve-cell adhesion and plasticity. It was reported to activate the FGF receptor.
Studies are in cultured neurons and rodents, covering memory, ageing and Alzheimer's-type models. No human trials or appearance data were found.
How it works: Reported to act as an FGFR1 agonist, promoting neurite outgrowth and neuronal survival in cultured rat neurons and changing synaptic structure in aged rats.
Risks and caveats: Human safety has not been established in published trials. It is not an approved drug, and animal findings do not establish human effects.
deepLead:
FGL (the FG loop peptide) is a 15-amino-acid synthetic peptide derived from the second fibronectin type III module of the neural cell adhesion molecule (NCAM). It was reported to activate fibroblast growth factor receptor 1 (FGFR1), mimicking part of the signalling that NCAM performs during cell adhesion .
Published research is preclinical: primary rat neuron cultures, and rodent studies of memory, social recognition, ageing and Alzheimer's-type pathology . No human clinical trial appears in the sources reviewed, and no data on appearance outcomes were found.
FGL is relevant to the wiki as a neuroactive peptide appearing in longevity and nootropic peptide catalogues; the sources reviewed contain no looksmaxxing community discussion of it.

name: Cenegermin

chain: Nerve growth factor on the cornea
angle.text: Cenegermin is a prescription nerve growth factor eye drop approved for neurotrophic keratitis, and it appears in peptide discussions as an NGF product. It has no documented appearance use; it is studied and approved for a rare corneal disease.

summary: A prescription nerve growth factor eye drop approved for a rare corneal disease, with no appearance use.
note: Approved only for neurotrophic keratitis; no cosmetic studies.
currentQuick:
Cenegermin (Oxervate) is a recombinant human nerve growth factor eye drop approved in the EU in 2017 and the US in 2018 for neurotrophic keratitis, a rare corneal nerve disease.
Trials in that condition showed most patients healing within about eight weeks. It is not an appearance product, and no cosmetic studies were found.
How it works: It acts on the TrkA and p75NTR receptors and was developed to address the nerve-related cause of corneal breakdown rather than only support the surface.
Risks and caveats: Reported adverse effects include eye pain, inflammation, tearing, eyelid pain and foreign-body sensation. It is prescription-only.
deepLead:
Cenegermin (brand name Oxervate) is a recombinant human nerve growth factor (rhNGF) given as an eye drop, produced in E. coli. It acts on the TrkA and p75NTR receptors and was the first drug approved for neurotrophic keratitis, a rare condition in which damaged corneal nerves lead to persistent epithelial defects . The European Union approved it in 2017 and the United States in 2018 .
In the registration trials, most adults with moderate or severe neurotrophic keratitis reached complete corneal healing within eight weeks, with healing rates generally higher than with vehicle . The most common adverse effects are eye pain, inflammation, increased tearing, eyelid pain and a foreign-body sensation .
Cenegermin is a medical eye treatment and is not described in the sources as an appearance product. It is included in this wiki because it is a recovery-category biologic; the sources reviewed contain no looksmaxxing community discussion.

name: Mecasermin rinfabate

angle.text: Mecasermin rinfabate is an IGF-1/IGFBP-3 injectable made for rare growth failure, and height-focused forum posters sometimes ask whether IGF-1 products could add height. That use is untested; it was studied only in children with growth disorders, and no data support height gain in people with normal growth.

summary: An IGF-1/IGFBP-3 injectable built for rare growth failure; no data supports height gain in people with normal growth.
note: Withdrawn for short-stature indications; no data for normal-height use.
currentQuick:
Mecasermin rinfabate (Iplex) pairs recombinant IGF-1 with its binding protein and is injected under the skin. Insmed developed it for children with severe IGF-1 deficiency.
It was withdrawn for short-stature indications after a patent settlement, and trials moved to muscular dystrophy and prematurity conditions. No studies address height in people with normal growth.
How it works: Binding IGF-1 to IGFBP-3 was designed to extend how long IGF-1 stays in circulation and to reduce side effects such as low blood sugar.
Risks and caveats: Reported effects in trials included lab changes such as higher testosterone and LDL in myotonic dystrophy patients. It is a prescription biologic, and published safety data come from patient populations.
deepLead:
Mecasermin rinfabate (brand name Iplex, also called rhIGF-I/rhIGFBP-3) is a complex of recombinant human insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1) bound to recombinant IGF binding protein 3, given by daily subcutaneous injection. It was developed by Insmed to prolong the half-life of IGF-1 and potentially reduce side effects such as hypoglycemia .
Its original target was growth failure in children with severe primary IGF-1 deficiency or growth hormone insensitivity . According to Wikipedia, the product was withdrawn from the market for short-stature indications following a patent settlement, and research moved to other conditions .
Clinical work in the sources covers myotonic dystrophy, Duchenne muscular dystrophy, retinopathy of prematurity and other conditions . It is discussed in this wiki because of interest in height and bone growth; the sources contain no data on use for height in people with normal IGF-1 and no looksmaxxing forum discussion.

name: Axokine

angle.text: Axokine is a CNTF-based injectable developed as an obesity drug to reduce body weight through a leptin-like mechanism. It was discontinued; trials showed small weight loss, with antibodies developing in most users, and it is mentioned mainly as a historical fat-loss compound.

summary: A discontinued CNTF-based injectable for obesity that produced small weight loss in trials and triggered antibodies in most users.
note: Never commercialised; antibodies in about 70 percent of trial participants.
currentQuick:
Axokine is a modified version of CNTF, a nerve survival protein, that Regeneron developed for obesity after weight loss was noticed in an earlier trial.
In phase III trials the effect was modest, and most participants developed antibodies. It was not commercialised.
How it works: It was designed to lower body weight through a leptin-like mechanism, and in diabetic mice it was reported to raise metabolic rate beyond its effect on food intake.
Risks and caveats: Antibody formation against the drug was the major issue reported in trials. It is not an approved or marketed drug.
deepLead:
Axokine is a modified recombinant form of human ciliary neurotrophic factor (CNTF) that was developed as an obesity drug by Regeneron Pharmaceuticals. It carries a 15-amino-acid C-terminal truncation and two substitutions, and is reported to be more potent and stable than natural CNTF . It was designed to reduce body weight through a leptin-like mechanism .
The weight-loss effect was discovered when CNTF given for motor neuron disease caused unexpected weight loss . In phase III obesity trials around 2003, the average effect was small. According to Wikipedia, patients without antibodies lost about 12.5 pounds over a year versus 4.5 pounds on placebo, while nearly 70 percent developed antibodies to the drug after about three months . It was not commercialised .
Axokine is not an appearance product or a looksmaxxing staple; it is included as a historical fat-loss compound. The sources contain no forum discussion of it.

name: KTTKS

angle.text: KTTKS, sold as Matrixyl in palmitoylated form, is a collagen-signalling peptide used in anti-wrinkle skincare to smooth fine lines. It has a modest split-face trial, with open questions about how well it penetrates skin.

summary: The collagen-signalling pentapeptide behind Matrixyl, with a modest split-face trial and open questions about skin penetration.
note: Skin penetration is debated in the literature.
currentQuick:
KTTKS is a five-amino-acid peptide, usually attached to a palmitoyl fat chain and sold as Matrixyl in anti-wrinkle products since 2000.
A 93-subject double-blind split-face study of pal-KTTKS in photoaged facial skin reported improvement, and lab studies show it raises collagen production in cultured cells.
How it works: It is a matrikine, reported to stimulate extracellular matrix and collagen synthesis in skin cells; the fat chain is meant to aid penetration.
Risks and caveats: The sources reviewed do not report safety problems. Reviewers discuss whether enough peptide reaches the dermis, and it is sold as a cosmetic ingredient.
deepLead:
KTTKS is a pentapeptide (lysine-threonine-threonine-lysine-serine) used in anti-wrinkle skin care, usually in its palmitoylated form, palmitoyl pentapeptide-4 (Pal-KTTKS), sold under the trade name Matrixyl. Sederma launched Matrixyl in 2000. It is classed as a matrikine, a messenger peptide that regulates cell activity .
It was designed as a topical agent to stimulate collagen production. In a 12-week, double-blind, placebo-controlled, split-face study of 93 women aged 35 to 55, pal-KTTKS was assessed for improvement in photoaged facial skin . Laboratory work shows C16-KTTKS stimulates collagen production in human fibroblasts . Questions about how well the peptide penetrates skin are discussed in the literature .

name: Palmitoyl tripeptide-38

angle.text: Palmitoyl tripeptide-38 (Matrixyl Synthe'6) is a cosmetic signal peptide sold as a collagen booster to reduce wrinkles and firm skin. The evidence for that use is mostly supplier data and multi-ingredient serum studies.

summary: A branded cosmetic signal peptide sold as a collagen booster; the evidence is mostly supplier data and multi-ingredient serum studies.
note: Human studies test whole formulas, not the peptide alone.
currentQuick:
Palmitoyl tripeptide-38 is a lab-made peptide added to anti-wrinkle serums and creams. The supplier says it prompts skin to make more collagen and hyaluronic acid.
Most efficacy numbers come from the manufacturer. Independent studies test finished products with many ingredients, so the peptide's own contribution is not separated out.
How it works: It is described as a matrikine mimic: a fragment-like signal meant to trigger the skin's matrix-building cells. A palmitoyl fatty chain is attached to help it mix with skin lipids.
Risks and caveats: A 55-person patch test of one serum containing it reported no irritation. It is a cosmetic ingredient, not a drug, and long-term data specific to the peptide are limited.
deepLead:
Palmitoyl tripeptide-38 is a synthetic lipopeptide used as a cosmetic anti-wrinkle ingredient. It is sold by Sederma, a subsidiary of Croda, under the trade name Matrixyl Synthe'6, and is described by the supplier as a matrikine mimic, meaning a small signalling fragment intended to prompt the skin to remodel its extracellular matrix .
Its marketing rests on the claim that it stimulates production of collagens I, III and IV, fibronectin, hyaluronic acid and laminin-5. The most detailed efficacy figures available come from supplier-described testing (a small double-blind study of 25 women using a 2% cream), as reported in an AI-generated encyclopedia summary; independent peer-reviewed trials of the isolated ingredient were not located .
Published human studies that include the peptide test finished serums or moisturizers containing many other active ingredients, so effects cannot be attributed to the peptide alone . It is a cosmetic ingredient and is not a drug.

name: Glycyl-prolyl-hydroxyproline

angle.text: Gly-Pro-Hyp is a collagen-derived tripeptide found in oral collagen supplements, which people take for skin firmness and wrinkles. It is absorbed in animals; human skin trials have used collagen hydrolysates, with none of the peptide itself.

summary: A collagen-derived tripeptide found in supplements; absorbed in animals, with no human skin trials of the peptide itself.
note: Evidence for appearance use is essentially absent for the isolated peptide.
currentQuick:
Gly-Pro-Hyp is one of the small peptides produced when collagen is broken down into the hydrolysates sold as supplements.
Research so far covers how it is measured in products and how collagen hydrolysate is absorbed in rats. Human skin studies of the isolated tripeptide were not found.
How it works: After oral intake, hydrolysates are reported in rats to enter the blood partly as intact peptides. Whether this changes skin in people is the claim made for supplements, and it is not shown for this peptide alone.
Risks and caveats: No safety data specific to the isolated tripeptide were found. It is not a regulated drug.
deepLead:
Glycyl-prolyl-hydroxyproline (Gly-Pro-Hyp) is a tripeptide made of glycine, proline and hydroxyproline, a sequence characteristic of collagen. It is found in collagen hydrolysates, the ingredient in oral collagen supplements and some cosmetic products, and is one of several small peptides studied as a bioactive component of those preparations .
Available sources describe its measurement and absorption in laboratory and animal work. No study identified here tests the isolated tripeptide for skin appearance in humans.

name: AHK-Cu

angle.text: AHK-Cu is a copper tripeptide marketed in hair-care products and discussed in appearance circles as a hair-growth ingredient, much as GHK-Cu is for skin. The evidence for hair growth so far comes from cell-culture research.

summary: A copper tripeptide marketed for hair growth, backed so far only by cell-culture research.
note: No human hair-growth trial found.
currentQuick:
AHK-Cu is a copper-bound three-amino-acid peptide sold in hair products and related to the better-known GHK-Cu.
The main published work is a lab study on cultured follicle cells. Human results are not available.
How it works: In cell culture, a tripeptide-copper complex was reported to boost fibroblast growth and VEGF, and to act on dermal papilla cells, the cells that steer hair follicle growth.
Risks and caveats: No human safety or efficacy data specific to AHK-Cu were found.
deepLead:
AHK-Cu is a copper complex of the tripeptide alanyl-histidyl-lysine, also called copper tripeptide-3. It is marketed in hair-care products and discussed in appearance circles as a hair-growth ingredient, in the way the related GHK-Cu is discussed for skin .
Published evidence is limited to a laboratory study on cultured human hair follicle cells. No human trial of AHK-Cu for hair growth was found.

name: LL-37

angle.text: LL-37 is the body's own antimicrobial skin peptide, and forum posters discuss it for clearing acne, healing skin and anti-aging. These uses are based on its immune biology and anecdote, with no cosmetic trials behind them.

summary: The body's own antimicrobial skin peptide, now chatted about for acne with no cosmetic trials behind it.
note: Not an approved drug; no acne or cosmetic trials found.
currentQuick:
LL-37 is a natural antimicrobial peptide made by skin and immune cells. Researchers study it mainly for its part in skin infection, atopic dermatitis, psoriasis and rosacea.
Some forum users ask about it for acne, but no human trial has tested that. The few registered LL-37 trials involve melanoma and diabetic foot ulcers.
How it works: It damages microbial membranes and attracts immune cells through the FPRL1 receptor. Vitamin D raises its production.
Risks and caveats: It is investigational. Wikipedia notes that excess LL-37 is suspected in rosacea and psoriasis inflammation. No safety data for cosmetic use were found.
deepLead:
LL-37 is a 37-amino-acid antimicrobial peptide and the only cathelicidin made by humans. It is cleaved from a precursor protein, hCAP18, and is produced by neutrophils and epithelial cells including skin keratinocytes . It is part of the innate immune system and also signals to immune cells .
In appearance communities it is sometimes discussed as a research peptide for acne or skin quality. Published work is predominantly on its natural role in skin infection and inflammatory skin disease, including atopic dermatitis, psoriasis and rosacea, rather than on LL-37 as a cosmetic treatment . No clinical trial of LL-37 for acne or cosmetic skin improvement was found.

name: Heberprot-P

angle.text: Heberprot-P is a Cuban injectable EGF used for diabetic foot ulcers, and it comes up in discussions of EGF for skin healing and renewal. Wound-healing evidence is small-scale and covers ulcers; nothing exists for cosmetic use.

summary: A Cuban injectable EGF for diabetic foot ulcers; wound-healing evidence is small-scale and nothing exists for cosmetic use.
note: Prescription wound drug; no appearance studies.
currentQuick:
Heberprot-P is an epidermal growth factor injection made in Cuba to treat severe diabetic foot ulcers.
Human reports are mostly small series and one registered phase 3 trial. No studies of cosmetic use were found.
How it works: EGF stimulates skin cell growth. In patients with ulcers it is injected into the wound base and edges to promote granulation tissue.
Risks and caveats: It is a medical product given by clinicians, not approved in the US as of 2016 per Wikipedia. Safety information in the sources reviewed is limited.
deepLead:
Heberprot-P is an injectable formulation of recombinant human epidermal growth factor (rhEGF, nepidermin) developed by Cuba's Center for Genetic Engineering and Biotechnology and marketed by Heber Biotec. It is used for advanced diabetic foot ulcers, where it is injected into and around the wound.
It is a wound-healing medicine. Its relevance to appearance culture is as an EGF product discussed among growth-factor skin and regeneration interests; no studies of it for cosmetic outcomes were found.

name: Palifermin

angle.text: Palifermin is a prescription keratinocyte growth factor approved for chemotherapy mouth sores, and it is occasionally mentioned in skin-renewal discussions because it stimulates epithelial cells. The evidence is for mucositis, with no cosmetic studies.

summary: A prescription keratinocyte growth factor for chemotherapy mouth sores, with no cosmetic evidence.
note: Label warns of possible tumor-growth stimulation.
currentQuick:
Palifermin is a lab-made version of keratinocyte growth factor given intravenously to protect mouth and gut lining in patients having intensive cancer treatment.
It is not studied for looks. Its approved use is oral mucositis in blood cancers.
How it works: It binds the KGF receptor on epithelial cells, which is reported to boost their growth, maturation and migration.
Risks and caveats: The label lists rash, fever, raised amylase, itching and swelling as common, and flags uncertain effects on tumors expressing KGF receptors and possible fetal harm.
deepLead:
Palifermin (brand name Kepivance) is a truncated recombinant human keratinocyte growth factor (KGF), a member of the fibroblast growth factor family produced in E. coli. It is approved to reduce the incidence and duration of severe oral mucositis in patients with blood cancers receiving high-dose chemotherapy with stem cell support .
It is a cancer supportive-care drug, not a cosmetic. It appears in appearance contexts only as a keratinocyte growth factor; the US label notes the KGF receptor is present in skin, hair follicles and sebaceous glands, but no studies for cosmetic use were found .
